# The talk {#sec-talk}

The script for **"Graph Embeddings 101, or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and
Love Claude Code."** The deck it goes with is `slides/lightning-talk.qmd`.

This is no longer a lightning talk. The earlier version of this chapter was a
seven-minute script and it is preserved in the git history if you want it. The
current talk runs **25–30 minutes** at a normal speaking pace, with four parts:

| Part | What it is | Minutes |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Dr. Strangelove, Boston, bike lanes | 5 |
| 1 | Graph embeddings, built up from "what is a graph" | 12 |
| 2 | The drug knowledge graph demo in R | 4 |
| 3 | How I actually use Claude Code | 5 |
| 4 | The Whitespace health check | 3 |

::: {.callout-tip}
## What to cut when you are running long

Cut **Part 0 down to the Strangelove slide and the parking-ticket line** — the
bike lane material is the most cuttable thing in the talk because it is pure
digression, which is also why it is the funniest. Decide before you walk on
stage, not during.

Inside Part 1, the compressible slides are *Which distance, though?* and
*When $A$ isn't enough: GNNs*. Do not rush Part 2; the analogy result is the
payoff for everything before it.
:::

---

## A note on the comedy

Three rules that this script tries to follow, because a technical talk that is
*trying* to be funny is much worse than one that isn't:

1. **The jokes are on the way to somewhere.** Every bit in Part 0 sets up a real
   idea. The bike lane is a distributed system with no coordinator. The freeze
   is a synchronisation failure. If a joke doesn't hand off to content, cut it.
2. **Undersell.** "Which is why every AI lab has a blog" works if you say it
   flatly and move on. It dies if you pause for the laugh.
3. **Be the butt of it.** The parking tickets, not knowing the material, the
   cherry-picked analogy. Punching at yourself is free; punching at the audience
   is not.

## The script

### Part 0 — Two minutes of unrelated grievances

#### The title is a reference

> The title is a reference, and if it isn't landing for anyone: *Dr. Strangelove,
> or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb*, Kubrick, 1964.
>
> Here is my favourite thing about that film. Kubrick set out to make a serious
> thriller about nuclear annihilation. He read the actual nuclear strategy
> documents — the real ones, the ones the RAND Corporation was writing — and he
> discovered they were already comedies. So he gave up and filmed that instead.
>
> I have had a similar experience reading AI discourse.
>
> The plot, in one sentence: the Soviets build a Doomsday Machine that destroys
> the world automatically and cannot be switched off. And it has exactly one
> flaw.
>
> *(beat)*
>
> They forgot to announce it. A deterrent nobody knows about deters nobody.
>
> Which is why every AI lab has a blog.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Say the last line flatly and go straight to the next slide. Do not wait.
:::

#### The bomb comparison

> Everybody reaches for the bomb comparison, so let me get it out of the way and
> at least be precise about which parts hold up.
>
> Holds: physicists knew roughly what it would do and built it anyway. "If we
> don't, they will" is doing an enormous amount of load-bearing work in both
> eras. And the people closest to it are the most nervous — that part is
> genuinely eerie.
>
> Doesn't hold: the Manhattan Project was about two hundred people and one
> government. It did not ship as a twenty-dollar-a-month subscription. And
> nobody had to explain Trinity to their parents at Thanksgiving.
>
> Also, Oppenheimer got "Now I am become Death, destroyer of worlds."
>
> We got "You're absolutely right!"
>
> One serious note, and then I'll stop. In the film, "I learned to stop worrying"
> is sarcasm. The whole point is that you should not love the bomb. I'm choosing
> to read my version straight. Ask me again in five years.

#### Hi, I'm Adam

> Quickly, who I am. I'm new to Boston — I moved here from the Netherlands.
>
> Last week I went to the DMV to get my license. Before that I collected two
> parking tickets, for parking outside my own house. While moving into it. With
> the boxes still in the car.
>
> So I asked the guy at the DMV: genuinely, what's more expensive — the tickets,
> or just paying for parking?
>
> *(beat)*
>
> "Paying for parking. Welcome to Boston."

#### The bike lanes

> I want to be fair about this. For an American city, Boston is genuinely not
> bad. That is the nicest available sentence and I have thought about it a lot.
>
> But here is a Dutch bike lane in cross-section. Three separate places, at three
> different heights, in three different colours. Cars, kerb, bikes, footpath. No
> negotiation required, because the negotiation was done once, in concrete, in
> 1975.
>
> And here is the American version. One flat surface. The bike lane is a paint
> colour. And it is stored between moving traffic and the doors of parked cars —
> which is, and I want to be clear about this, the two most dangerous available
> locations, chosen simultaneously.
>
> It's also where the delivery van goes. And the police car. And the cones.

#### It's not the infrastructure

> But the lanes are the easy half. The hard half is that in the Netherlands
> everyone knows the protocol.
>
> A pedestrian hears a bike coming, so they keep walking. The bike routes around
> them. Nobody makes eye contact. It just flows. It's a distributed system with
> no coordinator and it's genuinely beautiful.
>
> Here, someone steps into the bike lane, sees me coming, and —
>
> *(beat)*
>
> freezes. In the bike lane. Full eye contact. Waiting for **me** to decide what
> happens next.
>
> And I've come to think this is the most American thing I have ever
> experienced. A total stranger, in a moment of real physical danger, has
> concluded that the correct move is synchronous negotiation.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
This is the biggest laugh in Part 0 and it is the one to protect. It works
because "synchronous negotiation" is the room's own vocabulary being used on a
person standing in the street.
:::

#### Anyway

> Anyway. We're here to talk about graph embeddings.
>
> And, apparently, Claude.

### Part 1 — Graph embeddings, from nothing

#### A confession

> A confession before we start. Until I began writing this talk, I knew very
> little about graph embeddings.
>
> I didn't pick the topic because I'm an expert. I picked it because I wanted to
> become one, and agreeing to give a talk is the only reliable forcing function I
> have ever found.
>
> Which I think makes this a better talk, not a worse one, because I still
> remember which parts were confusing.
>
> And I learned it from Claude, which is a genuinely excellent teacher.

#### How I actually study now

> Here's the loop. Open-ended conversation about a thing I don't understand.
> Then: turn that into a Quarto book, one chapter per idea, runnable code in
> every chapter. Then: write me a lecture script from chapter three. Then that
> script goes through the ElevenLabs API and I listen to it on the way in.
>
> On the T. Not on the bike. I'm not doing the bike lane thing again.
>
> The step that matters is *runnable code in every chapter*. A book that only
> produces prose will happily explain something false to you for forty pages,
> fluently, with excellent grammar. Code that has to run is a lie detector.
>
> Here's fifteen seconds of a synthetic voice that sounds suspiciously like a
> certain Oscar winner, patiently explaining the Riesz representation theorem to
> me at 1.4× speed.
>
> *(play clip, cut it early)*
>
> Donald knows what I'm talking about.

#### What is a graph?

> Right. From the top.
>
> A graph is a set of nodes and a set of edges. That's it. That's the whole
> object.
>
> Here's the one everybody uses: thirty-four people in a karate club in the
> 1970s, and who was friends with whom. The club had a falling-out and split in
> two, and the question people have been asking of this dataset for fifty years
> is whether you could have predicted the split from the friendships.
>
> Now, a natural question. Is this a metric space? And I think probably yes,
> right? Because we can define a distance. A metric is any function on pairs
> that's non-negative and zero only on the diagonal, symmetric, and satisfies the
> triangle inequality.

#### Which distance, though?

> The trouble is that lots of functions satisfy those axioms and they disagree
> with each other.
>
> Shortest path — fewest hops. Fine, but it's integer-valued and on a real
> network everything is between two and six, so it barely discriminates.
>
> Commute time — how long a random walk takes to get there and back. That uses
> *all* the paths rather than just the best one, which is usually what you
> actually want.
>
> Resistance distance — treat the graph as an electrical circuit. Beautiful, and
> it degrades badly on large sparse graphs.
>
> And then: count the mutual friends. Which is not a metric, violates the
> triangle inequality, and is embarrassingly hard to beat. Remember that one.
>
> So we do have a metric space. The problem was never that we lacked a distance.
> The problem is that a distance is not a coordinate. `lm()` cannot take a
> distance. Neither can a neural network. They want a row of numbers.

#### What is an embedding?

> So: what's an embedding? Precisely, it's a map from nodes into R-to-the-d — a
> vector space representation of your points — with the property that close in
> the vector space means structurally close in the graph.
>
> d is small. Sixteen to two hundred and fifty-six. Fixed, dense, and independent
> of how many nodes you have.
>
> Here's the karate club, embedded in two dimensions. The colour is the faction
> each person actually joined. The algorithm never saw the labels. The first axis
> alone gets thirty-three out of thirty-four right.
>
> And that's the part that still surprises me: the representation ends up meaning
> something.

#### king − man + woman

> Everyone has seen this. King minus man plus woman is approximately queen.
>
> Nobody asked for that. Nobody added a "royalty" column. It fell out of a model
> trained to do nothing but predict nearby words. Which means the space has
> directions that correspond to concepts.
>
> Obligatory honesty, because I promised myself I'd say this: the example is
> somewhat cherry-picked. The original code excludes the input words from the
> answer, and if you don't exclude them, the nearest vector to king minus man
> plus woman is very often just king.
>
> The phenomenon is real. The demo is polished. We're going to reproduce it on a
> graph in about eight slides, with exactly the same caveat attached.

#### Why not one-hot?

> Let me ask the room something. If you want to feed a node into a neural
> network, how else might you do it?
>
> *(take answers — one-hot is the one you want)*
>
> Right, one-hot. Node seven becomes a vector of zeros with a one in position
> seven. It works.
>
> It's also the least informative thing you could possibly write down. It's n
> columns wide, so it changes shape when someone joins the club. And the distance
> between any two distinct nodes is root two. All of them. Every pair, equally
> far from every other pair. There is no geometry in it at all.
>
> An embedding carries much more than a one and a pile of zeros.

#### Basis vectors

> And in a way this is really a question about choice of basis.
>
> Quick review. A basis is a minimal set of vectors that spans the space, so that
> every point is exactly one weighted sum of them. Changing basis doesn't change
> the space. It changes the coordinates — and it changes which questions are
> easy.
>
> One-hot *is* a basis. It's the standard basis, e-one through e-n. One axis per
> node, n dimensions, maximally uninformative.
>
> Spectral embedding is also a basis — the eigenvectors of the Laplacian, keeping
> the d smoothest ones.
>
> So we are picking a basis that means something. And we would like to pick a
> good one: few coordinates, and the ones you keep should line up with things you
> care about.

#### Word to vector

> So how do you get from a word to a vector? Word2vec, 2013: predict a word from
> the words around it, throw away the prediction, keep the weights. The weights
> are the embedding.
>
> There are many algorithms. The one from Stanford is GloVe — Pennington, Socher
> and Manning, 2014 — and it takes a completely different route: build the full
> word co-occurrence matrix, then factorise it.
>
> Hold on to that pairing. Sample the neighbourhood, versus factorise the
> co-occurrence matrix. It comes back in six slides.
>
> Both of them rest on one sentence from a linguist in 1957: you shall know a
> word by the company it keeps.

#### Now do it for a graph

> Now: how would we do the same thing for a graph? We need an algorithm that
> maps the structure — nodes and edges — to a vector. And unsurprisingly there
> are many ways.
>
> And there is a direct analogue of word2vec, and the trick is almost insultingly
> simple.
>
> A random walk on a graph is a sentence.
>
> That's it. Take random walks. Write down the nodes you visit, in order. You now
> have a text corpus where the words are nodes. Run word2vec on it, completely
> unmodified. That's DeepWalk, 2014.
>
> Sixty lines of base R. And nothing in it is order-n-squared, which is exactly
> why this is the family that scaled to graphs with billions of edges.

#### Factorise something

> Here's the other route. You want connected nodes to be close, so penalise every
> edge by the gap it stretches. Write that down, and the sum turns into f
> transpose L f, where L is the Laplacian.
>
> Minimise it, constrain it so it can't collapse to a constant, and you get the
> eigenvectors of the Laplacian with the smallest eigenvalues. The smoothest
> non-constant functions on the graph. Four lines.
>
> Free bonus: a gap in the eigenvalues tells you how many communities there are.
> Three near zero, then a jump. Three communities. Nobody told it three.

#### They're all the same algorithm

> And here's the thing I actually found startling.
>
> DeepWalk is not really a neural method. Skip-gram provably converges to a
> factorisation of a pointwise-mutual-information matrix — that's Levy and
> Goldberg, 2014 — and for random walks that matrix has a closed form. Qiu et
> al., 2018.
>
> So every method on this slide is a low-rank factorisation of a matrix built
> from the adjacency matrix. They differ only in *which* matrix.
>
> Which is the same sample-or-factorise pairing as word2vec and GloVe, with the
> same punchline: it doesn't much matter which you pick.
>
> Here they are side by side. Same accuracy. About a thousand times faster.
>
> So before you reach for a library: try an SVD.

#### GNNs

> One more, quickly, because you'll be asked about it.
>
> Everything so far is a function of the adjacency matrix alone. Which means it
> can't use node features, and it can't embed a node that wasn't there when you
> trained.
>
> GNNs fix that by replacing the lookup table with a function of the
> neighbourhood. The weights are shared, so a brand-new node is just a forward
> pass.
>
> Two things to know. A GCN layer is a learned smoother — stack twenty of them
> and every node converges to the same vector, which is why GNNs are two or three
> layers deep and everyone is oddly quiet about that.
>
> And a graph attention layer is just self-attention masked by the adjacency
> matrix. That's the whole idea.

---

### Part 2 — The demo

#### A drug knowledge graph

> Let's do an actual example in R.
>
> This is a small drug knowledge graph. Twenty-four drugs, each joined to its
> molecular target, its pharmacologic class, and the conditions it treats — and
> those are joined to a body system. Fifty-five nodes, ninety-four edges.
>
> The important constraint: no drug is ever joined directly to another drug. So
> every similarity you're about to see has to travel through the structure.

#### Nearest neighbours

> First, the easy question. What's nearest to metoprolol?
>
> Its two fellow beta blockers. Then the class node. Then the receptor all three
> of them bind.
>
> It recovered "beta blocker" without ever being told that drug classes exist.

#### The analogy

> Now the fun one. I was genuinely curious whether this would work, and I want to
> be honest that I didn't know the answer when I wrote the slide.
>
> Same arithmetic as king minus man plus woman. The question is whether "this
> drug, but for a different disease" is a *direction* in this space.
>
> Atorvastatin, minus high cholesterol, plus depression.
>
> *(reveal)*
>
> Fluoxetine. Prozac. Top of the list — then sertraline and citalopram, with the
> serotonin transporter all three of them bind wedged in between.
>
> One more. Lisinopril, minus hypertension, plus type two diabetes.
>
> Metformin. Which is first-line therapy for exactly that.
>
> Nobody put a "first-line therapy" column in this graph. There is no such
> column. There are only edges.

#### Before anyone gets excited

> Now let me take that away from you a bit, because I'd rather do it than have
> someone do it in the Q&A.
>
> This graph is clean by construction. I wrote it. Every class has exactly three
> interchangeable drugs, which is precisely the parallel structure the
> parallelogram needs. Real clinical vocabularies are not this tidy.
>
> It's fifty-five nodes. The function is choosing among about fifty candidates,
> and node type alone rules out most of them.
>
> And drug repurposing by vector subtraction is a real research area. It does not
> work this cleanly. If it did, we'd be finished.
>
> What I'd actually claim is narrower and still interesting: the geometry is
> doing something real — it found drug classes out of nothing but edges — and
> analogies are a fast, cheap way to *inspect* an embedding and see what it
> learned. Not to make clinical decisions with.

### Part 3 — The Claude Code part

#### One thing to understand

> Okay. A few notes on actually using this thing.
>
> If you take one idea away, take this one: you are managing a fixed context
> window, all the time.
>
> That's the whole mental model, and everything else follows from it. It is not a
> database and it is not a colleague with a memory. It is a very good reasoner
> looking at a fixed-size window of text that *you* chose.
>
> So the entire skill is being deliberate about what's in the window. Which means
> you want to be dynamic about what you load — not everything, all the time.

#### CLAUDE.md vs skills

> Which is the difference between the two mechanisms people confuse.
>
> `CLAUDE.md` is "add this to the beginning of every conversation." Always
> loaded. You pay for it on every single turn. Good for how you like code
> written, your house style, the two commands that are never in the README.
>
> A skill is "load this when it's relevant." It's a folder with instructions and
> a one-line description. The description is always visible; the body only gets
> pulled in when it's needed.
>
> That's the actual unlock, and it took me a while to see it. It isn't *more*
> context. It's the *right* context, on demand.
>
> A four-hundred-line `CLAUDE.md` is a tax you pay on every message and mostly
> don't use.
>
> And memory works at both levels — global across every project, and local to
> one.

#### Why the terminal changes it

> The other thing, and this is the big one. A chatbot can tell you what to type.
> This reads files, writes files, and runs commands.
>
> Which sounds incremental and really isn't, because it closes the loop. It can
> check its own work. Write the code, run the code, read the error, fix the code
> — with no human in the middle copy-pasting tracebacks.
>
> Every number on the last fifteen slides was produced that way. Including the
> ones that came out worse than I hoped, which are still on the slides.

#### Things I've actually done

> A few things I've actually done with it.
>
> Reproduced a paper. Multi-armed bandits, from the PDF to a working simulation
> that matched the published figures.
>
> Written a course — this one. Quarto book, eight chapters, every number computed
> at render time.
>
> Written lecture scripts and image prompts, pushed them through the ElevenLabs
> API, and made myself an audio course I listen to on the way in. You can teach
> yourself basically anything while walking around, which still feels vaguely
> illegal.
>
> The general shape is that it adds context to anything, and it organises and
> connects ideas that were sitting in different places in my head.
>
> And if you take one workflow: open-ended conversation, turn it into a
> structured markdown file, build a project around it. The conversation is where
> you work out what you think. The markdown file is where it stops evaporating.
> The project is where it has to survive contact with a compiler.

### Part 4 — The bit

#### A language with no visible syntax

> Last thing. Another thing you can do is write code in languages no reasonable
> person would use.
>
> Donald told me about one. He called it something I probably shouldn't say into
> a microphone.
>
> It's actually called Whitespace. Edwin Brady and Chris Morris, 2003. The entire
> syntax is space, tab and linefeed — every visible character is ignored, which
> means a program can hide inside perfectly ordinary text.
>
> It's stack-based and Turing complete. Arithmetic, heap storage, subroutines,
> jumps, character and numeric I/O. All of it.
>
> And when you open the file, you see nothing. It isn't obfuscated and it isn't
> minified. It is illegible in the strict sense — there's nothing there to read.
>
> I should say, I've already been corrected on this and I deserved it: it isn't
> "all spaces." Tabs and linefeeds are load-bearing. A language of nothing but
> literal spaces would need something external, like run lengths, to encode
> anything at all.
>
> Three characters. Which is two more than I was hoping for.

#### Choosing the target

> So obviously we started thinking about what we could write in it.
>
> We wanted the smallest program that is absolutely critical to every
> tech-forward company on earth and that nobody has opened in six years.
>
> Not the payments code — people read the payments code. Not auth — people
> definitely read auth. We wanted something that returns the same three bytes,
> forever, to a caller that is not a human.
>
> *(beat)*
>
> The health check endpoint.
>
> It returns "OK". Every load balancer, orchestrator, uptime monitor and deploy
> gate on the planet is downstream of it. It was written by an intern. Its last
> commit message is "fix".
>
> If it stops returning OK, the entire company is down. And the file has
> forty-five bytes in it.

#### So we wrote it

> So we wrote it. Here it is.
>
> *(beat — let them look at the blank column)*
>
> That's the whole program. That's not a placeholder, that's the source.
>
> Here it is again with dots for spaces and arrows for tabs. Push seventy-nine,
> print it. Push seventy-five, print it. Push ten, print it. Exit.
>
> And it runs. There's an interpreter in the repo, forty lines of Python, and the
> health check passes.
>
> And because every visible character is ignored, you don't even need a
> suspicious blank file. You can paste those forty-five bytes into the trailing
> whitespace of the README and it still runs.
>
> Ship it on a Friday. Nobody finds it for years.

#### Takeaways

> Four things.
>
> Graph embeddings turn structure into geometry. A graph is already a metric
> space; what it's missing is coordinates. An embedding is a choice of basis, and
> a good one puts the things you care about on the axes.
>
> They're all the same algorithm — a low-rank factorisation of a matrix built
> from A. Sample it or factorise it, you get the same answer, and the SVD is a
> thousand times faster. Try an SVD before a library. And always run "count the
> mutual friends" as a baseline, because it wins more often than anyone admits.
>
> The geometry means something. Nearest neighbours found drug classes; analogies
> found first-line therapies. Out of nothing but edges. And stay suspicious of
> how clean my example was.
>
> And manage the context window. `CLAUDE.md` is always-on, skills are on-demand,
> and the terminal is the thing that lets it check its own work.
>
> Everything's in the repo — book, code, slides, the drug graph, and yes, the
> health check.
>
> Thank you. Please don't stand in the bike lane.

---

## Questions you will get

**"Doesn't node2vec do better than DeepWalk?"**
: Sometimes, on some graphs, after you tune $p$ and $q$ — which is two more
  hyperparameters and a grid search. @sec-walks has the comparison. The
  honest answer is that the gap is usually smaller than the gap between "any
  embedding" and "no embedding".

**"Why not just use a GNN for everything?"**
: If you have node features or need to embed unseen nodes, do. If you have
  neither, a GNN on a featureless graph is an expensive way to compute
  something an SVD gives you in a second.

**"Is the analogy result real or did you fish for it?"**
: Both, and say so. The two on the slide are the two I tried. The graph is one I
  wrote, with deliberately parallel structure. That is exactly what the "before
  anyone gets excited" slide is for — get there before they do.

**"What's the catch with Claude Code?"**
: It is confidently wrong at a rate that would be disqualifying in a person, and
  the entire discipline is building loops that catch it — tests, running the
  code, rendering the book. That's why "runnable code in every chapter" is the
  load-bearing part of the workflow and not a stylistic preference.
